segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The following tape was recorded on the 3rd of July, 1973, on the porch at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Marvin Long. The voices on the tape are those of Marvin Long or Marsha Long, his wife Martha, and Rob Moore, the interviewer. The Longs live in the residential section of Kendrick, Idaho, in a house built by the original draftsman of the town plat for Kendrick, a man named Kirby. Background noise is the traffic on the street outside the Long home.

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: And he had a number of business, what we call his useful business ventures that are really interesting considering he's a, well now you're junk business, you know that is. Is that on though?

segments.words: I think so. Let me see, yeah it's going. Well tell me about your junk business.

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Let's see, when was that back in? Let me get this picture. What year was I sick? Well anyway I was sick a year I'd been working store all morning. You were about 21. 21. And I was sick a whole year of nervous breakdown. And the first time I got up with my clothes on I weighed 101 pounds so you might know it. Right. And all I had was debts but when I was a kid I bought junk and sold it. And I started out and I had a, see did I have a horse? I had a horse, one horse, my neighbor over here. He had one of these democrat wagons, you know what a democrat wagon is? It's one of those small, just a small wagon.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Why was it called a democrat wagon?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah the little one.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Why was it called a democrat wagon?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: I don't know. I don't know but that's the nickname for it. It's a small wagon. You know there was two types, there was the big ones they hauled rain in, you know, the forest team should go and then they had this little one for delight work, you know, run around. These little wagons. Anyway I went over there and least rented this wagon and I had a horse and I think I paid him a dollar and a quarter a day to rental instead of renting a car. Right. And I went out buying junk and I made this whole territory home country and I must have worth about $300 anyway when I got through.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of junk were you getting?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: At that time it was hides and horse hair from the farmers they saved. Well it occurred you didn't know how the tails were made. That was a good price but you didn't get them with the weight of it. Hides and brass, copper and rubber, the whole rubber chunk. I was a regular. Wool too. Yeah, wool, anything, you could get a market for it. And I cleaned up and paid all my expenses that summer. I owed $300.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Where did you peddle the stuff?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: I had a stated trip in a fur company, they're own business in Spokane. I had a method, the buyer come down every Saturday and bought it and shipped it to Spokane. I had a good market for all that stuff. How long did you stay out on these trips to the ridges? I stayed out a week… friday.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you usually travel along one ridge on a trip?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah, I worked them all. I worked everything along here. I didn't miss any places. I got a lot of free to meal, a lot of sleep, I didn't sleep in Wagon Island every night. They just brought me in. I stayed one place, stayed a whole week, one place, they wouldn't let me go anywhere else.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How long did you stay in that business?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, that summer, until I got out of debt.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Then you went back to work in the store again?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah, I went back to the store. Yeah, just to get out of debt, I couldn't know a dollar. Yeah, people were good to me though. And then he's outdoor, was recommended, you know, when he was well. Well, you know, most of you know I weighed 101 pounds.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, was the store a better business than the junk business? Well, that's when you went to school, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah, I was just a kid. I was working for wages and stores. I never got into this. I went back into this. I came back here in 1920. I was 26 years old when I went into the books and business. Of course, I stayed with them until I was the last one left. There were three of us brothers, my dad and I, when we originally started. Of course, we had, we did farm, had cattle, slaughterhouse, grocery store, and we had some rice goods and meats.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How did the store business change over the years, you know, like as things changed, you know, as cars came in?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, as the cars came in, people come to town off there and bought smaller orders and competition becomes more and more competitive. They didn't drive to Lewiston or Moscow or wherever it is at, in horse and buggy days, but that's when the cars come in, you had to get more competitive. They didn't go like they do now, but they still went. Of course, it probably don't make any difference where you're at nowadays with the cars. The distance from Moscow to Lewiston to Kendrick is the same distance as from Kendrick to Lewiston, did you know that? Well, there's little, what I'm getting at is a little business sense to that too. See, there's so much, two points for me, how far it is back and forth. Well, I had, I worked up quite, I knew quite a few people here that went to Lewiston and worked, everybody goes to Lewiston and works a job, you don't have to ask them where they're working because they went down and worked for the Potlatch Forest, because that's our payroll. Well, I got a bunch of new ones down there and they'd come up on Saturdays and kept increasing, and they'd come up on Saturdays and put their work put. Now Lewiston, that works both ways, if you're a car driver, you got a Fox-AMC, so it can be done, I found that out.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, when people started, people started traveling more and you had to compete more, did you kind of change, you had to change your way of doing business, change your line of goods?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Like how?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, just not get stuck with anything, that's what I was, you know, what people wanted.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Now there's just certain things, they come up here from Lewiston and there's things I was special in, we worked shoes and gloves, see?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: I had to know what they wanted, those were the boys from the mill. And if you carried it and you had your prize and didn't market, and most of these business firms, even Penny and all those guys, it's a one-way street, you know, and their markup isn't flexible, you know.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And that's why, if you find out what their markup is, how good it is, how you can beat them, see?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Find out what they're making a profit on, just you stick with me to death, even Penny, find out what they're making a profit on, all them change you. Just get under them. Give them some of their own medicine.

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long

segments.speaker: Rob Moore

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Oh, yeah, that's all I mentioned.

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, how long was this cattle country? What? How long was this cattle country? What do you mean, how? Well, until when?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Until it was more cattle raised around you. Still, cattle, big range back there in the mountains, still lots of cattle, but not like those in those days. segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What was it like here in your store during the big depressions, 28, 29?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: It was a barter deal, he couldn't barter, he couldn't trade while he was out of the picture, he just couldn't make it. There wasn't any money, see, and you just had to, can you? Of course, we had to have a certain amount of money, but I'm sure it was a trade deal.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, we, sure, we'd trade for anything that we could sell, anything they'd have. segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: But then you'd trade that on again to somebody else who wanted it?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: But you kept going through the Depression just by trading?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long

That was the end. Tell me about the dry goods. That first store, how big it was. Yardage, ready to wear for women. Men's tailored suits that were ordered and all that was done right in that store. segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: And, he'd come in and he'd, I think it was five or six boys, wasn't it? Oh. They're all grown now, and these kids had got family. Anyway, he brought these sticks in. Mm-hmm. segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: He just didn't have these clothes to come in and it just, he was that kind of a guy. Mm-hmm. He was paying for them shoes and he was buying them. Mm-hmm. Didn't have any chance. segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was that around the Depression times?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah. Mm-hmm. We were back there when we first came to Canada and jumped through the Depression. The Depression done, I guess that's what done away with it. Mm-hmm. segments.words: Well, after you've gone out and made this money, what did you usually spend it on?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, I'll tell you, we wasn't getting very big money. Mm-hmm. Dad was pretty good to us. He wouldn't make us, unless we was working on some good job or something, he wouldn't make us. I paid one little one. Mm-hmm. You know that when I was working studying in the store, and getting paid for the month. That's when I was sick and buying that junkie temperature, I think. Mm-hmm. By the time you've bought your clothes and paid board, if you was working out, you couldn't have too much to worry about. Yeah. And we, of course we had to have a weekend, but every week or two, there was dances. Mm-hmm. Nice to go to.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did they have fiddlers come down and play the dances, or local people?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: They had orchids… they had rag arts, good music. We had a lot of good music here in town. I don't know, it was pretty fortunate.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Mostly local people?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Oh, yeah. See, we had a Thomas family, we used to live right over there and they were gone musicians. Well, this Walt Thomas, he went and spoke to the band leader up there and was doing the army. He wanted to enlist in the army in the band. The army said, well, they couldn't take any enlistments. Of course, they hadn't got any leaders, they didn't have any band leaders. They didn't take any leachates. Well, he says, I'm your man. He says, I'm a band leader. He took his examination down. He left this band all the time, all the ones he went overseas with.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: I don't know, that was World War I, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah. Yeah, he went overseas with his band.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: They used to play, what kind of music would they play for dances? What? What kind of music would they play?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Oh, mostly violin, piano.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Square dance type tunes or polkas or what?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, not much square dance in those days, Roger. Mostly, when I danced with them, my dance was mostly waltzes, waltzes and two steps. And by theirself, they'd have a cadre or whatever it was. What did they call that, quadrilles? What was it… i think so...… i wasn't there...… no… didn't have any more school systems in those days. No.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: This was probably quite a bit quieter back then, too, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Oh, that's right… there's much streets, there's much streets. Horses. They have more sidewalks.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The sidewalk was that high?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah, come right off the edge or... By the street.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: I guess it was a little bit quieter then, too, wasn't it… that's quieter?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah. Oh, yeah. They had a shivaree or something. There were a bunch of drunks sometimes. Yeah. Yeah, pretty quiet. Horses don't do this. Well, I've seen the first cars, motor cars, come in this country.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Where do they come from?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, they ship them. Oh, four-wheelers.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: You've seen the picture? Well, I think the one we, the dealer here, I think it was International. I think they were.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: A dealer came into town to start selling cars?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: No, there was a dealer here. These hardwares, the ones that sold them… didn't they… see that… there was a four-wheeler and a one-seated buggy tire. And one-seated. Did you ever see one of the old ones?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Yeah, I think I have. What were people's reactions to the first cars that came in here? What did they think of them?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: They were excited… you know, and you'd get killed going up and down these grades, you know, and all that stuff. Yeah. See, once they got killed, first thing they knew everybody was dying. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did the first ones come in by train or did they drive in by themselves or what?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: I don't remember. Well, they were shipped. I imagine the distributor of Moscow, I imagine. No, they didn't get so many out in the first thing. People didn't buy them. They'd buy them now… see that… a fella got a car to run a, well, he generally had some kind of a commercial car. He wouldn't be buying one. You know, just to go out and buy a car. Most of them were commercial cars.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: You mean cars that people run their businesses with or what?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, yeah, for delivering, you know, and stuff. The one they started to come, they come pretty fast. Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: About what year was that? Oh, no, what year would that have been?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Let's see, we come down here in 1908. The very first one around that time, I think. See, World War I was 18, wasn't it? 18 to 20? Just before World War I. About in there is when it started. I think.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did the wars have any effect on life out here besides, you know, having something else to read in the paper?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, I'll say. World War I, putting everybody had somebody over there fighting. Mm-hmm. Dad couldn't go out to work. He'd walk cattle here and stuff. He had a brother over there, front line trenches in World War I. He couldn't leave this town until the paper come in about 9 o 'clock to get the daily paper and read that casualty list. That's how much he was worried about. Just see whether Tom and Brother Tom had spared another day or not. It was awful. What they went through with, the grandparents. Mother seemed to take it a lot better than Dad did. Dad didn't take it. He couldn't take it. Well, it was an awful thing. Mm-hmm. You know, you'd have to have a son over there in the trenches in order to realize it, wouldn't it? Mm-hmm. Some of them. Some of them was filling their pockets and that was good to see. Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was that even happening out here? What? The filling your pockets?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Sure. Sure. There was everywhere. What kind of businesses out here could profit by... Well, there's some of them. Raising prices. Wheat. Wheat went up. They was praying for wheat to go up. Mm-hmm. The more they killed over there, the more wheat it took, see… isn't that something… yeah. That's very... One guy was mourning over his son being over there in the trenches and the other one was glorifying him because he was keeping his sweet price up. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did that same thing happen in the Second War?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Not as bad, no. It didn't last very long. Well, it lasted about six years.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: War II?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah. The war wasn't as rough either. The memorial to the boys of the First World War was the flagpole in the cart down here. Mm-hmm. And they moved it just this last year and the big metal ball on top contained a list. Huh. Yeah. They didn't replace that. They moved it over by the Second War Memorial there on the corner. The swimming pool at the memorial for the Second World War. There's a big box with all the names of the boys on the corner there. And this first one, a copy of the Gazette with all their names was in that ball on the top of the flagpole. They gave the ball to get over here pretty easy. Huh. I think. Where did they put the ball back? I don't think they put it back. I think he's got the paper in the way that was in there… see, who's that… that's one. Okay. That takes a lot of effort. Oh, it takes a lot of effort. You've got it out there. Oh, it's okay. There's a girl that lives in here going, you know, she's a fool or something. She don't have any set though.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What have we covered at this point? What other stories did you tell me before we started the machine run? You haven't told me. I'm trying to recall now. You haven't said much about the time you spent when you were homesteading up, was it around Leland that you were homesteading?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Dad homesteaded when he come out here in 88. He come out and homesteaded up here on Cedar Creek. Took out a timber. They called it them days, a stone timber claim. The homesteads. He had the rights to do that… and, let's see… and he made his living by making shakes and peddling them out on the farmers on Potlatch Ridge.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How long was he out there?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, he was up in ... He come in 88 and one day he was up in this place. In 88. You were real small. Well, let's see. He was born in 94.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Why did he give up the homestead?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Because of the bettering himself. He come out and rented a farm on Potlatch Ridge.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: That was the apple farm?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: No, that was a grain farm. And he got, it seemed so bad that he had to quit farming. And we went to Leland. We got meat business.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you prove up a rock and timber claim the same way you proved up a regular homestead?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah, if you wanted to take it. You could develop it if you had the right. At that time when he come in here, if he got out here on the ridge, he could have got some of this farmland. And you just waited until somebody throwed it up. You could get a homestead and a stone and timber and a preemption. You had three rights when they first come in here. They were that eager to get settlers.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What was the preemption?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, it was just a, I don't know exactly what it is, but we took up some of the best land we was taking up out of the farm. It was a preemption. I just never quite understood what that is. It wasn't the old time, they should have told me, I guess. But anyway, that's what we could have. And some of them got some of this stone and timber. They just had a few stones on it and a few trees. They called it stone and timber and got by with it. They got pretty strict on that. But this preemption was, I don't understand it, I know of one outfit up there on the Potlatch Ridge, one of these huffins. They were really big there, these grandparents. They took up preemption in homesteads. And they got control of a lot of land up there. And I guess the Stellas and some of them were families yet. But that's what they had. That's how eager they were to get people to develop this country. Of course, I think that stone and timber was abused by privilege.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What were you supposed to do with the stone and timber?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: You had certain improvements you had to make on it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What's the difference between stone and timber in a regular homestead?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: A regular homestead was anything. This farmland up here was all come under homesteads. But on the edges up there, they'd take fringes. That's where the fringes come in. The stone and timber is where you developed the stone or timber. Oh.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Like you were supposed to quarry stone or do some logging or something?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: If it was that kind of a stone, we didn't have any right in here. But there is sections that do have a church. Well, around the mining countries, there's a lot of that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Could you get more land on the stone and timber thing or what?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: The homestead gave you 160 acres. All right. Your preemption gave you 160 acres. And then your regular homestead. I gave you stone and timber, didn't I? Then your regular homestead gave you three quarters if you were in a position to accept it. And of course, some of them were.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: You had to develop different things on each section.

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: I think then if you pull some strings or something too, it had something to do with it. I noticed most of them had that all and was pretty badly criticized by the old-timers. I don't just understand it too much.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Where were the people? Your dad just had the stone and timber though, right? Or did he have more than that?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Well, no. I think he took up, I think, under just the homestead. I don't think he ever took any stone and timber. But he could. That's the opportunity. I guess what I was telling you when this came in, that he had an opportunity to get a stone and timber and didn't take it. And you'd always regretted it. You didn't use up that right. Because it wasn't long afterwards that you couldn't do it anymore. But he could have had those. You see what I mean? And people did take it. They'd prove up, live so long on this, and then come out and get a stone and timber. And do the same thing on it. Right. Yeah, see three rights. What did I say? Stone and timber and homestead… preemption. Preemption, yeah… then you lived in Leland and your mother ran a hotel. And what'd your dad do there? That's when you had the meat market. We run the cattle and the meat market. We peddle meat. We cut it up. We put up ice in the wintertime. And these meat wagons would build the boxes on behind these hags. And then it was placed down in the bottom for ice. And we'd ice them up in the morning. And take out this, cut this meat up and peddle it all over the Potlatch Ridge. And I was just big enough to go around looking for gates. Oh, I cut them in the meantime. We peddled it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would you take one row today or something? Would you have a regular route?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: We had routes… we had routes. We'd generally make six days a week. We'd generally have three routes and make them every other. See how that'd be? We'd make them every other day. But you could have made them pretty often. Didn't have any way of keeping them.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How would you keep your ice?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: We had ice houses. Did you ever see an ice house? Did you ever hear of one?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words:
I've heard of them. I've never seen one. 
Marvin Long or Marsha Long,0:52:08,Well… then you'd pack the ice in the meat wagon and pack meat boxes on top of that?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: We'd have the meat on trays and stuff and have this ice underneath. And this meat was all cut and put on trays. And they'd come out to get by and we had scales there. And they'd wait it on.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: By the pound rather than by the cut?

segments.speaker: Marvin Long or Marsha Long
segments.words: Yeah, by the pound. Took me along to open gates.
